passage:
In the girls' hostel of an engineering college, Ira had spent the day deciding: which elective to drop before the deadline, whether to fill the internship form, what to eat at the canteen when everything looked oily, which bus to catch for the lab.
At 9 p.m. her roommate Pema asked, "Coming to the club meeting? You said you'd sign up for the coding team."
Ira lay flat on her bed. "Maybe next week."
Then she opened a food delivery app, ordered a large cheese pizza she hadn't planned on, and watched episodes until one. The sign-up sheet closed at midnight.
In the morning she stared at the empty pizza box, puzzled at herself.

qa.q: When did the sign-up sheet for the coding team close?
qa.a: The sign-up sheet closed at midnight.

qa.q: Why did 'maybe next week' feel reasonable to Ira at 9 p.m.?
qa.a: After a day of deciding electives, forms, food and buses, one more choice felt too heavy, and lying down with easy episodes felt like rest she had earned.

qa.q: What could Ira do differently on a day full of decisions?
qa.a: She could sign up for the team in the morning while fresh, or ask Pema to walk her to the meeting, so the evening doesn't decide for her.

qa.q: How might Pema feel when Ira skips the meeting again?
qa.a: Pema might be disappointed or worried, having heard Ira say she wanted to join, and may wonder why she keeps backing out.

grounding: Shows a student who spends the day on decisions and in the evening drifts into impulse food and avoiding what she planned.

passage:
Hi Abhinav,
I owe you an apology for bailing on the study session again. I didn't have a real reason, so here's the honest version.
Every day this semester I'm making a hundred small choices: which lecture to attend when two clash, what to eat on a tight budget, whether to take the morning or evening lab slot, which flat to see for next year.
By seven in the evening, when you texted about the session, I just couldn't decide anything more. So I didn't reply, told myself I'd answer later, and ended up buying a second plate of samosas and scrolling videos until two.
Can we fix a standing time, Tuesdays at six? That way there's nothing to decide.
Yusuf

qa.q: What time did Abhinav text about the session?
qa.a: Abhinav texted at seven in the evening.

qa.q: Why did Yusuf not reply to Abhinav's text, from Yusuf's point of view?
qa.a: After a day of a hundred small choices, even saying yes or no felt like too much, so putting it off to 'later' felt like relief.

qa.q: Why is a standing Tuesday time a smart choice for Yusuf?
qa.a: It turns the study session into a fixed routine, so tired evening Yusuf doesn't have to decide anything to show up.

qa.q: How might Abhinav feel reading this email?
qa.a: Abhinav may feel less hurt once the reason is clear, and perhaps relieved to have a fixed plan instead of waiting for replies.

grounding: Shows a student who, worn out by many daily choices, avoids an evening plan and falls into impulse snacking and scrolling.

passage:
Himani, you asked why I didn't reply to the landlord all week. Okay, listen.
My days are choice after choice. Wake up: which class first, the one with attendance or the one I actually need? Lunch: mess or the stall, and can I afford the stall? Afternoon: group project, where everyone wants me to pick the topic, the slide colours, the deadline.
By evening, the landlord's message, "Sarita, about renewing the rent agreement...", is sitting there, and it's a big decision, so I just close the phone. Put on a video. Eat whatever's in my drawer. Tell myself, tomorrow.
It's not laziness, I think. It's like the part of me that chooses has clocked out for the day.

qa.q: What was the landlord's message about?
qa.a: It was about renewing the rent agreement.

qa.q: Why does ignoring the landlord feel reasonable to Sarita by evening?
qa.a: Sarita feels drained and overwhelmed by evening, after a day of choices about classes, lunch and the project, so a big decision like the rent agreement feels impossible, not lazy.

qa.q: What would you advise Sarita to do about the landlord's message?
qa.a: Pick a fresh morning slot, like before the first class, to read the agreement and reply, instead of facing it at the end of the day.

qa.q: What might the landlord think after a week of silence?
qa.a: The landlord may think Sarita is not interested or is being careless, and could start looking for another tenant.

grounding: A student describes how a day of small decisions leaves nothing for a big one in the evening, so the big one gets put off.

passage: I'm Ayesha, and I share a PG room with Kavitha, a second-year law student. Her mornings are all decisions: which lecture to attend when two clash, whether to take the moot court slot, poha or eggs at the mess, which bus to catch. By lunch she's comparing internship forms on her laptop. Then something changes around eight at night. Yesterday her project partner called three times about Saturday's meeting. Kavitha watched the phone light up and turned it face down. She ordered fries for both of us on a food app without reading the menu, then scrolled short videos until one. I can't say what goes on in her head. But when I asked about the partner, she only said, "Tomorrow. I can't pick a time right now." This morning she answered the call before breakfast and settled it in two minutes.

qa.q: What did Kavitha do when her project partner called last night?
qa.a: She watched the phone light up and turned it face down.

qa.q: What does Kavitha's line "I can't pick a time right now" suggest about how she felt at night?
qa.a: It suggests she felt too drained by a whole day of choices to make even one more, so putting it off felt like relief rather than laziness.

qa.q: Which choice this morning made the difference, and how could Kavitha use it again?
qa.a: Answering the call before breakfast let her settle it in two minutes; she could keep small planning calls for mornings instead of late evenings.

qa.q: How might Kavitha's project partner have read her silence last night?
qa.a: The partner may have felt ignored or worried that Kavitha didn't care about the project, since they couldn't see how worn out she was.

grounding: A roommate watches a student who makes many choices all day slip into avoidance and impulse ordering at night.

passage:
Monday: Minakshi's first term at university in Melbourne was a string of choices: which tram, which tutorial, which cheap lunch, whether to join the cricket club, how much to spend on groceries. At nine that night her flatmate Bhavna asked, "Coming to the club trial on Thursday?" Minakshi said, "Don't know," and ate biscuits for dinner in front of a show.
Wednesday: Worse. An email from her tutor about a missed quiz sat unopened. At eleven she bought a jacket online that she didn't need.
Saturday: Over chai in the morning, Minakshi wrote a short list with Bhavna watching: same lunch every weekday, same tram, and one "decision hour" at ten each morning. Then, still in that hour, she opened the tutor's email, replied, and signed up for the trial.

qa.q: What did Minakshi buy online on Wednesday night?
qa.a: At eleven she bought a jacket online that she didn't need.

qa.q: How did Minakshi seem to feel on Monday and Wednesday, and what shows it?
qa.a: Minakshi seemed overwhelmed by so many choices, answering "Don't know" about the club, leaving the tutor's email unopened and buying a jacket she didn't need.

qa.q: What was the turning point on Saturday, and why could it work?
qa.a: Fixing lunch and the tram and keeping one morning decision hour cut the small choices, so she had energy left for the email and the trial 👍

qa.q: What was it like for Bhavna to hear "Don't know" on Monday night?
qa.a: Bhavna may have felt brushed off or unsure whether Minakshi wanted to come at all, without seeing how tired Minakshi was.

grounding: A student worn out by many daily choices defaults to snacks, impulse buys and unopened emails in the evening.
